tldr: This study introduces a World Action Model (WAM) that transfers the dynamics prediction capabilities of large-scale video generation models to robot control without the heavy inference-time cost of rolling out future videos, fully open-sourcing the model alongside a unified 20K+ hour open dataset and a fast training and deployment infrastructure.
hero_caption: An overall view of InternW0-Δ. It is pretrained on 23,072 hours of multi-source data combining real robot demonstrations, UMI data, and egocentric videos. With an MoT architecture bridging video and action experts and Causal Imprint, it achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse simulation benchmarks and four real-robot platforms.
overview:
World Action Models (WAMs), which leverage the predictive knowledge of "how the physical world changes" learned by large video models for robot control, have drawn significant attention. However, predicting and generating high-fidelity future videos is quite different from dexterously moving a robot. Most prior WAMs either rely on heavy diffusion models to explicitly roll out (generate) future videos during inference to infer actions, or simply co-train video generation and action prediction in parallel. As a result, they fail to obtain effective predictive representations that directly connect captured future changes to action generation.

To address this, the authors developed "InternW0-Δ". It bridges a video expert and an action expert via a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT). To eliminate future video generation at inference time, it introduces a novel mechanism called "Causal Imprint," which learns "how the scene will change" from training-only future supervision and directly provides predictive representations to the action expert. Furthermore, it distills geometric and motion priors from a pretrained 4D foundation model to strengthen the physical insight required for action generation.

To power this framework, the authors unified over 15 open datasets—including real-robot manipulation logs, egocentric human demonstrations, and UMI data—into a canonical 80-dimensional state-action space, constructing a massive corpus exceeding 20,000 hours. In evaluations, it demonstrates superior robustness far surpassing prior methods on challenging simulation benchmarks like LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin 2.0, EBench, and RoboDojo. It also proves the effectiveness of zero-shot pretraining and real-time control across four real-robot platforms, ranging from bimanual parallel grippers to high-DoF dexterous hands.
contributions: Proposed Causal Imprint, a novel mechanism that extracts scene change representations necessary for actions from training-only future supervision and passes them directly to the action expert without rolling out future videos at inference time.

Constructed an architecture integrating a directed Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) combining video and action experts, training-only geometric and motion distillation from a pretrained 4D foundation model, and semantic understanding via a frozen static VLM.

Unified diverse open-source data—including real-robot demonstrations, UMI, and egocentric videos (such as Ego2Robot)—into a canonical 80-dimensional representation, establishing the largest pretraining dataset of its kind with over 20,000 hours alongside rigorous filtering pipelines.
Open-sourced the full system infrastructure, including pretrained weights, training and evaluation code, and an optimized inference runtime achieving a 152.8 ms round-trip latency on real robots.

sections.heading: Predicting the future without action? The WAM bottleneck and breakthrough
sections.summary: While World Action Models aim to transfer the physical knowledge of video prediction models to robot control, extracting action-relevant representations without heavy video generation at inference has been a long-standing challenge. InternW0-Δ achieves accurate and robust robot manipulation without generating future videos by combining a directed MoT, Causal Imprint, and 4D distillation.
sections.details:
Recently, World Action Models (WAMs)—which leverage the physical dynamics knowledge acquired by large-scale pretrained video generation models to control robot manipulation—have become an active research focus. However, there is a large gap between rendering visually plausible future frames and correctly controlling a robot. Driving a robot requires identifying task-relevant visual changes, understanding 3D and 4D geometry and motion, and deciding actions conditioned on the present scene.

Rolling out future videos online step-by-step with a diffusion model incurs excessive computational latency, breaking real-time robot control loops. Therefore, the core challenge is: how do we extract the video model's predictive power directly into action-guiding representations without the heavy burden of rolling out future videos?

InternW0-Δ tackles this by coupling a video expert and an action expert within a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) and introducing "Causal Imprint (Δ)," which provides future supervision only during training to distill latent scene changes. In addition, it distills geometric and motion priors from Track4World, a 4D foundation model, exclusively during training, boosting control performance without any inference-time overhead.

Furthermore, the authors unified diverse open data—including real-robot and human demonstrations—into a massive 20K+ hour training corpus, establishing a two-stage pretraining and downstream adaptation pipeline. It achieves remarkable results across simulators, such as LIBERO-Plus (92.8%) and RoboTwin 2.0 (71.9% under environment randomization), as well as four real-robot setups.

sections.heading: From VLAs to World Action Models: Trends and open foundations
sections.summary: While conventional VLA models integrate vision, language, and actions, WAMs deepen physical world understanding by connecting future visual prediction. InternW0-Δ advances the line of fast inference that foregoes future video rollouts, occupying a unique position by combining 4D geometric distillation with a large-scale unified open data approach.
sections.details:
### Vision-Language-Action (VLA) Models and World Action Models (WAMs)
VLAs like RT-2 and OpenVLA transferred the language and visual comprehension of pretrained VLMs to robot control, evolving into models generating continuous actions like π0 and GR00T N1. Meanwhile, WAMs such as DreamZero, Motus, and LingBot-VA emerged to model dynamic physical transitions beyond static visual recognition. Within this space, approaches like Fast-WAM—predicting future videos during training while bypassing video rollout at inference to emit only actions—have attracted interest. InternW0-Δ builds upon this philosophy while keeping the video expert trainable and introducing a novel directed connection supplemented by a static VLM for scene semantics.

### Visual and Geometric Representations for Robot Control
For robot manipulation, research has actively explored latent-space prediction (e.g., V-JEPA, VLA-JEPA) and geometric/motion priors such as point clouds and trajectory fields (Spatial Forcing, 4D-WAM, Track4Action). InternW0-Δ adopts a hybrid representation learning strategy: it explicitly trains latent future differences via Causal Imprint while distilling features from the pretrained 4D foundation model Track4World during training only.

### Open-Source Robotics Infrastructure
Efforts to release reproducible code and data pipelines, such as LeRobot, openpi, and StarVLA, are rapidly accelerating. Strongly aligned with this movement, InternW0-Δ provides a complete ecosystem: not just model weights, but standardization tools for over 20,000 hours of heterogeneous data, intermediate feature caching systems, and a high-speed inference runtime.

sections.heading: InternW0-Δ architecture: Imprinting future changes directly into actions
sections.summary: A video expert and an action expert are coupled via a 30-layer directed MoT, consuming only a sparse memory context (anchor, recent, and current frames) at inference. Causal Imprint bridges scene changes to the action side via latent differences and feature alignment; along with training-only 4D distillation, inference is completed with a single cached video prefill pass and fast action denoising.
sections.details:
### 3.1 & 3.2 Overall Architecture and Multimodal Encoding
The core of InternW0-Δ is the combination of a video expert based on the pretrained Wan2.2-TI2V-5B model and an ActionDiT (action expert) diffusion transformer. Multi-camera visual inputs are stitched into a single canvas image and encoded into latents via Wan's VAE. Robot states and actions are mapped to a canonical 80-dimensional vector and embedded via linear layers. For language instructions, the video expert receives Wan2.2's original T5 embeddings to maintain generative context, while the action expert receives output representations from a frozen VLM (RynnBrain1.1-2B) that concurrently interprets the current scene and the instruction.

### 3.3 Sparse Memory Context (SMC)
Maintaining all past frames densely causes computational costs to explode. Instead, this method adopts a sparse memory context retaining only three critical timestamps: the initial frame at the episode start (Anchor: A), the frame immediately preceding the prior action chunk (Recent: R), and the current observation frame (Current: C). This captures global task context and recent interaction history with minimal computation.

### 3.4 Causal Imprint
Causal Imprint (Δ) answers the question: "If we do not generate future videos at inference, how do we convey future predictive benefits to action generation?" Trainable tokens are added to the self-attention mechanism of the video expert to aggregate recent and current features. During training, these tokens are optimized with two objectives: a difference loss $\mathcal{L}_\Delta$ predicting the latent state change from current to future (e.g., $\Delta Z_t = z_{t+\rho_v} - z_t$), and an alignment loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}}$ matching representations from the video model's future layers. Consequently, while the token only attends to past and present information, it captures a rich summary of "how the scene will change."

### 3.5 Distillation of 4D Geometry and Motion
To further boost geometric and physical reasoning, the 4D foundation model Track4World serves as a teacher. During training, a 1430-dimensional geometric and motion descriptor extracted from the ground-truth video window is matched against a student descriptor—decoded from intermediate features (15th block) of the video expert via a 2-layer Transformer decoder—using an MSE loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{4D}}$. At inference, both the teacher and student decoder are completely discarded, incurring zero extra computation.

### 3.6 Directed MoT and Attention Masking
Both experts interact via shared attention layers, but the flow of information is strictly controlled by an attention mask. Future tokens can attend to past and current tokens to learn video generation, but Causal Imprint and action tokens are strictly blocked from attending to future tokens. The action expert only attends to current observations and Causal Imprint representations honed by future supervision.

### 3.7 & 3.8 Objectives and Ultra-Fast Inference Routine
The overall training loss integrates flow matching losses for video and action generation, the two Causal Imprint losses, and the 4D distillation loss. At inference time, future video tokens are never instantiated. Observation tokens (A/R/C) and Causal Imprint tokens are prefilled through the video expert only once, and their Key/Value (K/V) cache is preserved. The action expert denoises an action chunk (32 steps) from noise over several steps by attending to this cache. Because the video branch is never recomputed during denoising, execution is exceptionally fast.

captions.F2: The overall architecture of InternW0-Δ. Anchor (A), recent (R), and current (C) observations are encoded via VAE, while the Wan2.2 video expert and ActionDiT action expert collaborate via a 30-block directed MoT. T5 and a vision-language model (VLM) divide roles to supply language and scene contexts, while Causal Imprint tokens capture change prediction.
captions.F3: The distillation pipeline for 4D geometric and motion representations. Ground-truth descriptors extracted offline from Track4World (teacher) are matched with student features decoded from the video expert's intermediate layers. This branch is completely removed during inference, adding no extra computational overhead.
captions.F4: Structure of the World-Action MoT layer and attention mask. (a) Token types for video and action streams, (b) joint attention flow, and (c) attention mask visibility. Direct access from action (Act) and Causal Imprint (Δ) tokens to future (F) tokens is blocked, ensuring strict consistency with the inference setup.
captions.F5: Optimized inference execution flow. (1) Observations are encoded; (2) the video expert prefills A/R/C and Δ tokens once and caches the K/V pairs; (3) the action expert immediately generates a 32-step action chunk across N denoising steps by querying the cache without recomputing the video expert.

sections.heading: Unifying 20K+ hours of heterogeneous data: Canonical 80D representation and rigorous filtering
sections.summary: To uniformly handle diverse robot embodiments and egocentric human videos, the authors defined a canonical 80-dimensional state-action space with fixed semantic slots. Following thorough filtering against erratic jumps, static phases, and VLM instruction alignment, and incorporating the Ego2Robot pipeline to convert human video into robot trajectories via IK and inpainting, a 23,072-hour dataset was curated.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Canonical State-Action Representation
Directly blending diverse datasets risks assigning conflicting joints and coordinate frames to identical vector indices, destabilizing training. To prevent this, the authors defined an 80-dimensional standardized space with fixed semantic slots. The state vector holds joint positions, 3D end-effector (EEF) positions plus 6D continuous rotations, and gripper openings or multi-DoF hand joint angles. For actions, joint angles are expressed as absolute targets, while the EEF is expressed as relative displacements (3D translation + 3D rotation vectors) in the current EEF frame; dimensions absent in a particular robot are masked out.

### 4.2 Robot Data Curation and Rigorous Filtering
Fifteen open-source datasets covering bimanual arms, humanoids, and mobile manipulation—such as AgiBotWorld, InternData-A1, RoboMIND 2.0, and ABC-130K—were aggregated. They underwent a strict multi-stage pipeline: (1) anomaly detection and state-action directional alignment checks (filtering out trajectories with correlation below 0.65 or temporal drift), (2) trimming static phases at episode beginnings and endings, (3) visual quality filtering against dark frames, blur, and compression artifacts, (4) action threshold guards discarding wild steps (>0.2 m translation or >0.5 rad rotation per step), (5) instruction grammar curation via LLMs and automated video-instruction alignment checks via VLMs, and (6) visual validation using URDF renderings. This pruned the initial 13,867 hours into 11,302 hours of high-quality robot data.

### 4.3 Egocentric Video and the Ego2Robot Pipeline
To exploit egocentric human demonstrations (EgoDex, EgoVerse), an action alignment step was applied to estimate EEF positions and gripper states from hand geometry. Furthermore, the "Ego2Robot" pipeline solves collision-free robot joint trajectories in MuJoCo by coupling base placement search with inverse kinematics (Kinematic Alignment), masks out humans using SAM3, inpaints the background via ProPainter, and renders synthetic robot arms (Visual Alignment). Hand speeds were also halved to match typical robot dynamics, converting 1,101 hours of raw video into 5,633 hours of robot-equivalent training data.

### 4.4 & 4.5 UMI Data and Final Dataset Scale
Approximately 2,075 hours of Hy-UMI-10K (handheld camera and gripper data) were cleansed under equivalent standards. Ultimately, combining 11,302 hours of real robot data, 2,075 hours of UMI, 4,061 hours of raw egocentric human video, and 5,634 hours of Ego2Robot data yielded 23,072 hours of open training data (around 7 million episodes and 2.3 billion frames), representing the largest open-source corpus of its kind.

captions.F6: The Ego2Robot data conversion pipeline. Through three stages—Action Alignment (estimating 3D EEF position and opening), Kinematic Alignment (solving feasible robot motions via base search and trajectory IK), and Visual Alignment (removing humans with SAM3 and ProPainter and rendering synthetic robot arms)—human manipulation video is transformed into high-fidelity robot training data.

sections.heading: Two-stage training strategy: Scaling pretraining to diverse robot platforms
sections.summary: Pretraining was conducted on 256 A800 GPUs over 14 days on heterogeneous data to instill foundational visual dynamics and action generation. Thanks to the canonical representation, downstream adaptation to simulators and real-world robots requires only 10 to 15 epochs of fine-tuning from the identical pretrained checkpoint.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Large-Scale Pretraining Setup
Pretraining ran on 256 NVIDIA A800 GPUs with a global batch size of 4,096 in bfloat16 mixed precision for 245K steps (around 14 days). The data mixture consisted of 80% real-robot data, 10% Ego2Robot, 8% UMI, and 2% raw egocentric demonstrations, weighting the action loss accordingly (1.0 for robot, 0.5 for UMI, 0.1 for egocentric data). The video expert was initialized from Wan2.2-TI2V-5B, the action expert was initialized randomly, and the VLM (RynnBrain1.1-2B) was kept frozen. The first 235K steps trained on standard objectives, followed by the final 10K steps incorporating the Track4World 4D distillation loss.

### 5.2 Post-Training for Simulation
From the pretrained checkpoint, the model was fine-tuned for downstream simulators via dedicated adapters: mobile bimanual EBench (10 epochs), precision and memory-intensive RoboDojo (10 epochs), single-arm Franka LIBERO (15 epochs), and bimanual ALOHA RoboTwin 2.0 (10 epochs). All environments were tuned from the exact same pretraining checkpoint using identical hyperparameters, proving the versatility of the canonical space.

### 5.3 Post-Training for Real-Robot Deployment and RTC
Real-robot validation spanned four setups: two gripper platforms (ARX AC-One bimanual, Arx5 single-arm) and two dexterous primate hand platforms (Franka + XHand bimanual, TianJi Marvin + Wuji Hand). To bridge execution latency, the authors adopted Training-time Real-Time Chunking (RTC). By sampling an already-executed prefix action length $d$ (0 to 16 steps) during training, leaving that prefix uncorrupted as clean conditioning and denoising only the suffix steps, the policy reliably generates smooth actions continuous with preceding executions during live deployment.

sections.heading: System infrastructure optimizations: 3x faster training and 5x faster inference
sections.summary: To accelerate model exploration, the authors introduced a feature cache for frozen encoders and per-layer PyTorch Inductor compilation, improving training throughput up to 3x. For real-robot deployment, process isolation from ROS, K/V caching, and CUDA Graph optimizations reduced round-trip latency to 152.8 ms (5.11x speedup) on a single RTX 5090.
sections.details:
### 6.1 Training Infrastructure Accelerating Model Development
In research iterations, repeatedly recomputing heavy video VAE latents and frozen VLM tokens every epoch is highly wasteful. The authors developed a version-tracked "Cache Manager" that handles online and offline intermediate feature caching. Furthermore, by compiling the 30-layer MoT backbone layer-by-layer using PyTorch Inductor and leveraging FlexAttention, end-to-end training achieved speedups of 3.02x on LIBERO and 2.11x on RoboTwin.

### 6.2 Real-Time Asynchronous Execution and Inference Optimization
On physical hardware, an asynchronous pipeline runs at 30 Hz, replanning and inferring the next 32-step action chunk in the background every 16 steps (~533 ms). To reliably fit within this time budget, several core optimizations were applied:
- Complete process isolation of policy inference from ROS (rclpy) callbacks and Python GIL contention to avoid blocking CUDA kernel launches.
- Single-pass evaluation of observation embeddings and video expert K/V cache per step, which remain unchanged during action denoising and are reused across all denoising iterations.
- Grouped layer compilation for the action expert leveraging static tensor shapes and CUDA Graph Trees playback.

Thanks to these enhancements, the controller's round-trip time (RTT) on a physical dexterous hand setup powered by a single NVIDIA RTX 5090 dropped from 780.8 ms down to 152.8 ms, realizing a 5.11x speedup.

captions.F8: Architecture of the feature caching system. VAE latents and VLM context representations derived from training trajectories are stored in-memory and on-disk via the Cache Manager. Eliminating redundant computations from frozen encoders dramatically accelerates model development cycles.

sections.heading: Empirical results: Simulation robustness and real dexterous manipulation
sections.summary: In simulation, InternW0-Δ set new performance records on perturbed LIBERO-Plus (92.8%), RoboTwin 2.0 Clean2Random (71.9%), RoboDojo, and EBench. In real-robot trials, pretraining dramatically raised success rates, enabling adaptation to unseen liquid fill lines and fine fingertip tasks like pipetting and cup stacking with primate hands.
sections.details:
### 7.1 & 7.2 Simulation Benchmark Results
- **LIBERO-Plus**: In robustness evaluations featuring perturbed lighting, viewpoints, robot poses, and instructions after clean training, InternW0-Δ achieved an overall success rate of 92.8%, surpassing strong baselines like Qwen-RobotManip-Context (91.4%) and top WAM Being-H0.7 (84.8%).
- **RoboTwin 2.0**: Under the Clean2Random setup (training clean, testing randomized), it recorded 71.9%, outperforming prior WAM OpenWAM-α (48.7%) while maintaining 90.0% clean performance.
- **EBench & RoboDojo**: On EBench mobile bimanual tasks, it reached a top overall score of 66.0 (76.5 on long-horizon tasks). In the ultra-challenging RoboDojo, it achieved a 23.91% average success rate—nearly double OpenWAM-α (11.92%).

### 7.3 Real-World Robot Experiments
Across four hardware setups and 11 distinct tasks, pretraining showed drastic benefits: on AC-One, "Toaster Operation" jumped from 20% to 95%, and the "Luminol Experiment" soared from 0% to 95%. In a water-pouring task trained only on a single fill mark, the model showed qualitative generalization, adjusting its pour volume to match different target lines. Additionally, dexterous hands successfully executed delicate, highly coordinated motions, such as drawing reagents with a pipette and stacking cups.

### 7.4 Ablation Study: What Made the Difference?
A detailed ablation on LIBERO-Plus revealed individual module contributions:
- Sparse Memory Context (SMC): +3.88 points (49.59% → 53.47%)
- Static VLM (RynnBrain) semantic grounding: +15.61 points (53.47% → 69.08%)
- Causal Imprint (difference loss + alignment): +7.37 points (69.08% → 76.45%)
- 4D geometric distillation (Track4World): +1.92 points (76.45% → 78.37%)
Pretraining data ablations revealed that real-robot data yielded the highest gains, while egocentric human video benefited transfer most when kinematically and visually aligned to robot embodiments (as in Ego2Robot and UMI).

### 7.5 Runtime Assistance Exploration with Frontier Models
On difficult RoboDojo tasks, pairing InternW0-Δ with GPT-6 Astra as a runtime assistant providing global reasoning and action correction elevated average success from 10.80% to 47.20%. While the WAM alone handles low-level closed-loop control effectively, this demonstrates the promise of hybrid setups combining WAMs with external high-level reasoners.

sections.heading: Conclusions and outlook: Towards an open future for Physical AI
sections.summary: InternW0-Δ represents a milestone for World Action Models, bridging video dynamics directly to robot actions without inference-time rollout penalties. Open-sourced alongside a massive 20K+ hour corpus and fast infrastructure, it lays an essential foundation for physical AI research.
sections.details:
InternW0-Δ seamlessly fuses the predictive dynamics of large-scale video models with precision robot control via Causal Imprint and a directed MoT. By eliminating heavy video diffusion rollouts at inference, it reconciles real-time control constraints with broad environmental robustness.

Moreover, its engineering contributions—including standardizing over 20,000 hours of public data, feature caching, and compiled inference runtimes—offer immense practical value. All model weights, code, training recipes, and data processing tools are open-sourced.

As outlined in its limitations, future work must further clarify the optimal scaling and conversion strategies for egocentric human video, as well as systematically explore hierarchical planning architectures that combine WAMs with high-level agents like GPT models.

takeaways: A design that bypasses future video rollout at inference is essential for practical WAMs; Causal Imprint presents an elegant solution by imprinting future changes into current features using training-only supervision.

Language embeddings from video models (such as T5) alone are insufficient; coupling them with a static VLM that jointly interprets scene images and instructions yields massive task success gains (+15% or more).
Egocentric human demonstrations transfer far more effectively when aligned kinematically and visually to robot embodiments (e.g., via Ego2Robot) rather than supplied as raw footage.

System-level optimizations—such as frozen encoder caching, per-layer Inductor compilation, and process isolation—are just as critical as model architecture in enabling fast research iteration and low-latency (~150 ms RTT) deployment.
limitations: Raw egocentric human video does not yet produce dramatic improvements on current benchmarks, highlighting the need for deeper investigations into optimal scaling laws and embodiment conversion strategies.

Runtime assistance via frontier models like GPT was evaluated on limited tasks and trials; establishing systematic, autonomous hierarchical architectures between high-level agents and WAMs remains open for future research.
